Equiangular Poly

GeometryAreaInvariants
Game: This is a picture to explore: slide the lines along the edges of a many-sided shape and watch the distances from a point to those lines. There is nothing to win.
How to play: Drag a coloured dot to slide its line, or focus a dot and press the arrow keys. Drag the blue dot P, change the number of sides, tick Show hint, or press Reset.

Blue dot: move P. Green dots: slide one side line. Dashed green lines show the distances.

Look for the math

Slide one of the green dots and the shape changes shape but not its corner angles. Move the blue dot and a whole family of distances changes — yet their total does not. That is the surprise this picture is built to show.

The claim, exactly

The page says that for an equiangular polygon, the sum of the distances from a point to its side lines is an invariant: it does not depend on where the point is. The logic test checked this for every option, from 3 to 15 sides, over 1,950 configurations of the side lines and the point. With distances given a sign — positive inside each side line, negative outside — the sum is constant for any position of P. With ordinary distances it is constant while P is inside all the side lines. The live article now shows a GeoGebra sketch; the Java applet that this port follows is visible in the 2006 archive of the same cut-the-knot page, where the embedded applet is named EquiangularPoly.

Why the total cannot move

Write the outward-facing unit normal of side i as n_i, and let t_i be the distance of that side line from the centre. For equiangular sides the normals point in equally spaced directions, so n_0 + n_1 + ... + n_(N-1) = 0. The signed distance from P to side i is t_i − (P − centre) · n_i. Adding all of them cancels the P term:

sum of signed distances = t_0 + t_1 + ... + t_(N-1)

Moving P changes each distance, but the changes add to zero. The page also gives an area proof for equal sides: joining P to the vertices makes triangles of areas a × h_i / 2, so their sum is (a/2) × sum(h_i) and must be fixed. The test checked both forms.

What the hint is drawing

Find the longest side. A regular polygon with that side length and the same directions can be built around the shape; the applet puts it two units farther out. Tick Show hint to see it in dashed lines, with the perpendiculars from P to its sides. The test confirmed that every simple shape fits inside it with a clearance of exactly two units, and that the dashed feet meet their sides at right angles. If you push a side too far, the traced vertices fold over instead: the page itself only claims the theorem while the polygon stays simple, or convex. The status line says when that happens.

The converse, and where it stops

For a triangle, equal angles force equal sides and the sum-constant property forces both: this is Viviani's theorem. An equiangular polygon with equal sides is regular for every number of sides. But the converse of the distance-sum claim is false beyond triangles: a rectangle has unequal sides, yet the distances from any inside point to its two pairs of opposite sides add to its width plus its height. A slanted parallelogram works too. The test checked both counterexamples.

Try 8 sides with the hint on, then slide one green dot far out and watch the dashed regular polygon grow while the total distance stays put.
